# Canto 7: Accompanied by the Two Commentaries named Rasikapriya and Rasamanjari, Page 103

May this song uttered by Shri Jayadeva regarding Hari <gloss>Krishna</gloss> bring about the complete pacification of the sins of the Kali <gloss>the current age of spiritual decline</gloss> age. (Verse 8 of the 14th Song)

-> This moon, having the luster of the lotus-face of Murari <gloss>Krishna</gloss> which has turned pale through the pangs of separation, though it seems to mask my pain, spreads intense agony of love within my heart, for it is the friend of the Mind-born <gloss>the love-god Kamadeva</gloss>. (Verse 5) <-

The "battle of love" <note>original: rati-ranah</note>; in that state, she is steady and firm. (Verse 7) Regarding the phrase "uttered by Shri Jayadeva": may this play of the reversed encounter <note>original: viparita-tabhi-yoga-kriditam</note> bring about peace by calming the sins of the Kali age. (Verse 8) Thus it is said in the *Sangita Raja* <note>a 15th-century treatise on music and dance</note>: "Where the <term>Shri-raga</term> <gloss>a specific melodic mode</gloss> is used, the rhythm is the fast <term>munthaka</term>, the subject is the description of Vasudeva <gloss>Krishna</gloss>, and the actions are those of love-play, where the foot-sequences and the melodic extensions follow suit: that is known as the best of compositions <note>original: prabandha-varah</note>." This concludes the fourteenth composition named <term>Harimita-Champaka-Shekhara</term>.

Now Radha, distressed by separation, addresses the moon. "O friend," <note>original: aye, an address used in a soft or gentle tone</note>, "this moon spreads great love-anguish in my heart." What kind of moon? It is the friend and companion of the Mind-born <gloss>Kamadeva</gloss>. She says this while remembering the state of Murari <gloss>Krishna</gloss> during their separation. The moon possesses a luster like the lotus-face of Murari, which has become pale due to his separation from her. Therefore, even though it seems to cover or hide the pain <note>by its cooling light</note>, it actually increases the agony because of its friendship with the god of love. The meaning is this: Previously, though it removed my pain by appearing like the pale face of Murari during his separation from me, now, because it is the friend of Desire, it only creates pain. It has become unbearable; knowing that he is now attached to another, I cannot remain here. The term "leela-kah" refers to a playful swan. The dictionary *Amara* defines "lava-lesha" as a tiny drop in the ocean. (Verse 7)

Regarding "uttered by Shri Jayadeva": may the play of love belonging to Hari <gloss>Krishna</gloss> described by Jayadeva destroy the sins and impurities of the Kali age for the listeners and the readers. (Verse 8) Now she describes how even the moon causes her more suffering. "Oh" <note>original: aye, here used to express dejection or sorrow</note>, this visible moon expands the pain of love in my heart to an even greater degree. What is it like? It has the luster of the lotus-face of Murari <gloss>Krishna</gloss> which has become pale and grey due to the separation from me. The idea is that the sight of the moon, which looks like the lotus-face of Krishna, causes extreme pain by reminding her of that face. What is it doing? It is "covering the pain," meaning it makes it hidden or internal. By seeing the moon, one's discernment is uprooted, and the mind remembers only that Krishna who has committed an offense. He gives a reason for it being the cause of pain: "Mind-born" <note>original: manobhavah</note>. The moon is the friend of the Mind-born <gloss>Kamadeva</gloss>. The idea is that because I did not follow Krishna even though he was near, I have disobeyed the command of Love, and thus Love has become my enemy. The moon, wishing to help his friend, also causes me pain. The moon is known to be born from the mind of Krishna, and Kamadeva is also "Mind-born," so they are like brothers. The moon and Kamadeva share a natural friendship. As the scripture <note>the Purusha Sukta of the Rig Veda 10.90.13</note> says: "The moon was born from his mind, and from his eye the sun was born." The term <term>vedana</term> refers to both knowledge and pain, or it can indicate fear, anger, dejection, confusion, or remembrance. The term <term>tiras</term> refers to disappearance or moving in a crooked manner. (Verse 5)

<summary>Radha expresses how the moon, traditionally a cooling comfort, now increases her suffering because its appearance reminds her of Krishna's pale face and its mythological connection to the mind makes it an ally of the god of love.</summary>
<keywords>Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Radha, Krishna, Kamadeva, moon, separation, Rasikapriya, Rasamanjari, Sanskrit poetry</keywords>
